A family break in Northumberland: Why it’s an unforgettable UK holiday with kids

by Laura Riddell |
Updated on27th September 2026 at 4.46pm
Subscribe to our mag
Follow Take A Break on Google

c. Richard Riddell

Instaread

Northumberland is still one of England's great under-the-radar getaways - especially for families who default to Cornwall or Devon. Yet the North East delivers stretches of quiet beaches, storybook castles and unique heritage sites. Over the August bank holiday weekend, I headed up from London with my husband and our two young sons, Odhran, 11, and Reuben, 8, to sample a slice of this stunning region. Here are the places and activities we loved, and why Northumberland was absolutely worth the six-hour drive (even with kids in the back)....

c. Richard Riddell

Harry Potter broomstick training at Alnwick Castle

Alnwick Castle is one of the UK's best-known Harry Potter filming locations and you can enjoy Broomstick Training in the exact location where Harry had his first flying lesson in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. Fans (and adults can fly too!) will delight in recreating one of cinema's most iconic scenes, but you don't even have to be a Harry Potter enthusiast to enjoy this fun activity. Witchy professors provided entertaining instruction, and Odhran and Reuben smiled and laughed throughout the 25-minute experience, as they summoned their brooms and raced around before launch.

c. Richard Riddell

Broomstick Training sessions are free with a general admission ticket, but they are given out on a first-come, first-serve basis. Ask a member of staff or check on the 'What's On' board as you enter the grounds of Alnwick Castle, to find out where tickets are being issued for different time-slots (They're usually collected from the Artisans Courtyard).

c. Richard Riddell

The water features at The Alnwick Garden

It wasn't the warmest of summer days, but that didn't stop Odhran and Reuben whipping off their T-shirts and running through the water features at Alnwick Gardens. The Serpent Garden features mirror-polished, science-based water sculptures and Odhran was completely lost in his imagination, pretending to be a Chitauri (an extraterrestrial warrior from Marvel movies) pushing through Wakanda's energy shield barrier.

c. Richard Riddell

The centrepiece of The Alnwick Garden is the Grand Cascade with its timed water jet displays. And another highlight is the Poison Garden. Locked behind an iron gate, this is filled with around 100 toxic, intoxicating and narcotic plants. To enter the Poison Garden, you must purchase a general admission ticket to the gardens and book a guided tour slot, which costs an additional £1 per person. There isn't an age restriction, but this is probably more suitable for older kids, who can take in all the information.

c. Richard Riddell

The magical play village of Lilidorei

This fantasy play village of Lilidorei is like stepping into a storybook. It's home to nine clans of mythical creatures including elves, fairies, pixies, sprites and hobgoblins. They are ruled by Lord Elfwin, King of Lilidorei who lives in Elfin Drin, the biggest play structure in the world. This grand timber castle is the centrepiece of Lilidorei and it's main tower stands at 26 metres tall. An intricate network of smaller towers are connected through suspension bridges, gangways and secret tunnels, and after clambering to the top, kids can whizz back down on huge tube slides.

c. Richard Riddell

But surrounding Elfin Drin, is a village of quirky little huts, a wishing tree, and a host of colourful characters waiting to play. There are sandpits, swings and a little trail to follow through pathways lined by small Christmas trees. Visitors are allowed to bring a picnic, or there are food and drinks vendors and the kids enjoyed Troll Snot ice-cream. Lilidorei is located at The Alnwick Garden but you must purchase standalone tickets for Lilidorei or, for a couple of pounds more per person, you can purchase a combination ticket that allows you to enter The Alnwick Garden and Lilidorei.

c. Richard Riddell

Coastal foraging experiences

Northumberland is rich in edible plants, fruits, mushrooms and flowers, if you know where to look - and I most certainly wouldn't have had a clue without the expert guidance of Gemma, aka The Cramlington Forager, who leads seasonal wild food tours, explaining how to safely and sustainably gather and identify edibles. I'd imagined searching for mushrooms in woodland and berries in hedgerows, but Gemma met us at The Ferryman's Hut (widely considered the smallest museum on the UK) in the picturesque village of Alnmouth, to forage for surprising edibles along the coastline.

C. Richard Riddell

This was a unique sensory experience for the boys and helped to give them a deeper understanding and appreciation of the landscape. We sampled juicy samphire and seaweed pods growing in the tidal mudflats of Aln Estuary, before moving in among the sand dunes, where we uncovered everything from apple mint and rose hip to dead-nettles and sea buckthorn - little orange berries that apparently can be used to make a tasty sorbet! As Odhran pointed out, 'You'd walk by all these things and never really notice they were there.' Gemma opened our eyes to the bounty hiding among Northumberland's wild spaces.

c. Richard Riddell

Stepping into Victorian times at Heatherslaw Corn Mill

The North East has some wonderfully unique heritage sites, and among them is Ford and Etal - a 15,000-acre historic rural estate located in Northumberland. It features working farmland, charming villages, and heritage tourist attractions, including Heatherslaw Corn Mill, a fully working 19th-century water-powered mill that still grinds grain into flour. Odhran and Reuben enjoyed following a hidden mouse hunt trail, watching the 16-foot waterwheel through a glass walkway, stepping back in time to try on Victorian costumes, and testing out the interactive machinery - Reuben put some muscle into crushing grains between two heavy circular stones.

c. Richard Riddell

Our guide Sheila was so friendly with the kids. She had a passion for her job and was really informative. There's a little gift store, where you can buy flour produced by the mill. We took home a bag of Strong White Flour, and it made the most delicious scones and pizza bases.

Then we hopped on Heatherslaw Light Railway, a narrow-gauge steam train for a short but relaxing journey through the countryside to Etal, where we explored the ruins of a castle and stopped in for a drink at The Black Bull - Northumberland's only thatched pub.

c. Richard Riddell

Playing as Anglo-Saxons at Ad Gefrin

Ad Gefrin is an Anglo-Saxon museum and whisky distillery on the outskirts of the market town of Wooler (Gateway to the Cheviots). We entered into a striking golden domed foyer of carved wooden panels, designed to make you feel like you're stood inside a giant whisky barrel. Ad Gefrin whisky is crafted using local barley and water drawn from a borehole beneath the Ad Gefrin site in the Cheviot Hills. While my husband went on a distillery tour, I explored the Great Hall and Anglo-Saxon museum with Odhran and Reuben.

c. Richard Riddell

I was fascinated to learn about the Anglo-Saxon history of the area. In the 7th Century, the palace of King Edwin of Northumbria was located about four miles from the distillery but no one knew it's exact location until 1949, when an archaeology professor spotted crop marks from aerial photographs (you can see the aerial photographs in the museum). There's an immersive reimagining of a 7th Century Anglo-Saxon royal hall, where stories of kings and queens are brought to life through digital projections. The boys enjoyed dressing up as kings and sitting in their thrones. They played an Anglo-Saxon version of chess and engaged with interactive displays in the museum, which also held artefacts from the period, both from the original site and on loan from other museums. There was a member of staff who was super knowledgable and happy to answer questions and explain more about this period in history. It turned out to be helpful for Odhran and Reuben because as soon as they started back to school, they both happened to be learning about the Anglo-Saxons.

c. Richard Riddell

A Taste of Northumberland

In May, Visit Northumberland and Northumberland County Council launched a new Taste of Northumberland scheme, bringing together county-wide foodie experiences and tours with a new quality mark that assures consumers artisan skill and locally sourced products. It will help visitors easily identify authentic local food and drink and support businesses that champion Northumberland produce.

We stopped in at a couple of businesses that have signed up for the scheme. Bēodern at Ad Gefrin is a beautifully bright and airy restaurant with 270 light bulbs arranged to replicated the star constellations visible in the clear night skies above Northumberland. Seasonal menus highlight local produce, and here you're welcome to sit for coffee and cake, afternoon tea, or a three-course meal. We visited at lunch time and I enjoyed a main of roasted artichoke and pea risotto, whereas my husband and the boys ordered roast chicken breast with new potatoes, broccoli, yellow and green courgette, and chicken jus. If your child prefers something simpler, a separate children's menu offers chicken nuggets, fish goujons or a chicken burger, all served with chips.

For dessert, my husband and I shared Madagascan Vanilla & Tácnbora Whisky Crème Brulée and Seasonal Fruit Crumble with Tácnbora Whisky Crème Anglaise, while Odhran and Reuben chose a selection of ice creams from Doddington Dairy, which is based right next to Ad Gefrin. The food at Bēodern was delicious and well presented in beautiful earthenware. It was a really enjoyable meal in a calming atmosphere.

c. Richard Riddell

The Running Fox has five locations in Northumberland, but we stopped in at the Felton branch. It's a great breakfast or lunchtime spot, serving up a full English, a selection of sandwiches on artisan bread or traditional Northumberland Stottie, soups, pie, pastries, and a tasty selection of cakes and desserts - all homemade, using local ingredients. We were able to pre-order picnic boxes to take away, so we could enjoy eating lunch on the grounds of Alnwick Castle.

c. Richard Riddell

Stay at Percy Wood Holiday Park

This was one of the most peaceful holiday parks we have ever stayed at, and it felt so comfy to return here on an evening after a busy day exploring. We stayed in the two-bed Autograph Lodge with Hot Tub and it felt more like a cosy cottage than a lodge. The hot tub had been set up so it was the perfect temperature on arrival, and for someone accustomed to London's light pollution, it felt so relaxing to sink into the warm water under the dark Northumberland skies. It was fenced in, so it felt nice and secluded.

c. Richard Riddell

There was furnished decking out back for a leisurely breakfast, and the kitchen came equipped with everything we needed to cook and enjoy a relaxing night in. There's a bar and restaurant on site and there was a kids' disco on during our stay, but we preferred to chill in our comfortable lodge, which had wifi. We were able to connect our Fire Stick to the flatscreen TV to access our Disney account and watch movies. The lodge was spacious with a walk-in wardrobe in the main en-suite bedroom, so suitcases were neatly out of the way.

c. Richard Riddell

Percy Wood is a lovely tranquil retreat, surrounded by woodland, and it's only a 15-minute drive to Alnwick and nearby beaches. It's the perfect base for exploring this beautiful part of the country. Northumberland didn’t just give us a few great days out - it gave us the kind of family memories that follow you home, leaving us certain we’ll be back.
